In my history class, we covered the War of 1812 this week. One of the lesson objectives was to learn about the origins of the national anthem and the battle at Ft. McHenry. About three-fourths of my students are Mexican immigrants. None of them had ever heard the story about the song before. I taught them about the battle, where around 400 British ships (about two-thirds of their navy) surrounded and bombarded the fort. Francis Scott Key, an American lawyer, was onboard a British ship to negotiate a prisoner swap. I explained in detail how Key returned time and time again into the hold of the ship where the prisoners were being kept, all of whom wanted to know if the flag was still flying.

I told them about how I had the great blessing to actually see the flag at the Smithsonian and how it was tattered, torn, and riddled with holes from cannon fire--how it was much larger than you might imagine, and that it had fifteen stripes and stars. I explained how, when dawn came and the smoke cleared, the flag was still standing--that the Americans had prevailed. Then, after explaining all that in vivid detail, I quoted to them the verse of the poem that Francis Scott Key wrote, that became out nation anthem.

I pulled up scans from the National Archives and they could see with their own eyes, the actual page written in Key's own handwriting, written on the very day of the battle. I then shared with them Whitney Houston's performance of the anthem at the 1991 Super Bowl and I related to them how much that performance meant to me, because I was in the military at the time. It steeled the American people for battle at a time when we were still unsure that we were ready to fight a major enemy.

Next, I pulled up the lyrics of the song--the whole song, including the verses we never sing. The students got to see the stanzas that say "Thus be it ever, where free men shall stand between their loved homes and the war's desolation...Then conquer we must when our cause, it is just and this be our motto, 'In God is our trust." (Yes, I teach in a public charter school and I get a bit more leeway than in a typical public school.)

I explained to the students that some people want to replace the national anthem with a song like "America the Beautiful," because "The Star Spangled Banner" is a "war" song. I played the video of Beyonce singing "America the Beautiful" at Obama's inauguration. What did I hope to achieve with all of this? Most of these kids, who are first-generation Americans (anchor babies) don't know what being an American means. Throughout the school year, I have tried to teach them our history and teach why America is great. We have our flaws, but there is nowhere else on earth like this country.
